bearings.paper_claim: Proposition 2: if each threshold CDF F_j is concave on [0, +inf), the expected spread h(S) is submodular, so greedy selection applies. Corollary 1 (uniform thresholds, Eq. 6) gives a saturated coverage objective that is submodular. Lemma 1: influence maximization on the directed bipartite linear threshold graph is NP-hard, by reduction from Set Cover with thresholds alpha/2.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.2-4.3: Lemma 1 p.678; Proposition 2 p.678; Corollary 1 p.678-679; proof of Proposition 2 in Appendix A.2 p.684
bearings.system_side: lt_priming THETA ladder: deterministic constants from 0.6 (Highly Persuadable) to 3.0 (Opponent). prime() adds net_lean/120 and 0.25 per declared Opponent cell, sums P[u][v] times xf over pro sources, and solves each target separately for the cheapest mix of recruits and money. No seed-set objective is optimized.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/lt_priming.py: THETA about lines 20-21; prime() about lines 96-104
bearings.transfer_conditions: The concavity result transfers as mathematics only. Lemma 1 is an NP-hardness result for deterministic thresholds; the paper does not state a converse that missing concavity implies hardness. A point-mass (step) threshold CDF is not concave on [0, +inf), so the paper's submodularity guarantee does not cover lt_priming's deterministic thresholds if they were aggregated into a seed-set objective. Moderate for the mathematics, weak for empirical relevance.
bearings.verifier_note: Proposition 2, Corollary 1 and the THETA values, COMMIT=0.25 and the pressure sum were reproduced from the text and code. Softened: Lemma 1 is an unconditional NP-hardness result for the deterministic problem, not a dichotomy keyed to concavity. lt_priming also adds a lean term to theta, so theta is not purely the tier ladder.

bearings.paper_claim: Table 1: both InfMax methods beat Degree, Betweenness and PageRank in all 18 setups. The paper says both proposed methods beat all baselines in all but 3 of 18 setups. Pubmed GAT at 30 percent threshold: GC-RWCS 69.1, InfMax-Unif 64.1, no attack 85.2. In a 4-community SBM the better selectors spread seeds more evenly (qualitative).
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.2 Table 1, pp.680-681; Section 5.4 Figure 3, p.681
bearings.system_side: per_topic_coalition ranks neutral candidates by ev (engagement priority times delivery) and keeps the top 45, not by singleton marginal. Singleton marginal spread({n}) minus base is then computed over those 45 and used as the allocation weight, boosted by (1 + 0.8 times bpf). The 2M budget is water-filled with a 50k per-seed cap. The joint spread of the funded set is reported afterwards and does not shape the allocation.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/per_topic_coalition.py: lines 113-125 (cand top-45 cut, mg, boost, coal_waterfill, joint spread)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's objective is GNN misclassification on citation graphs at a 1 percent node budget. The CU objective is a Monte Carlo competitive cascade on the cosponsor kernel. The structural point transfers: weighting by singleton marginals ignores overlap, so funded seeds can cluster. The code already measures the joint-vs-naive gap. The community-spread finding is qualitative. Weak to moderate.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 1 numbers for the stand-alone baselines and the Pubmed GAT example were reproduced. The 3-of-18 count was not reproduced: the best of the two InfMax methods strictly beats the best baseline in 17 of 18 setups (only Citeseer GCN 10 percent fails); both methods strictly beat it in 14 of 18 (non-wins: Citeseer GCN 10, Citeseer GAT 10, Citeseer JK 10, Cora GCN 30). The system_side ranking claim is wrong: the top-45 cut uses ev, and singleton marginals only set allocation weights.

bearings.paper_claim: Corollary 1 Eq. 6 with a = 0.01 over B = M^L (L = 4) is a saturated coverage function and is submodular. The paper says this objective outperforms one-step and centrality heuristics. The paper's experiments compare against Degree, Betweenness, PageRank, RWCS and GC-RWCS; no one-step coverage baseline is tested.
bearings.paper_location: Corollary 1 Eq. 6, pp.678-679; Section 5.1 settings p.679; Table 1 pp.680-681
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit is cardinality-bounded (nSeeds), not cost-bounded as its comment says. Coverage cov = 1 - prod(1-p) is updated over DIRECT edges PE only, so coverage is one hop. Greedy marginal gain includes an optional target weight (1 + 2 dT) and a stance filter. The code comment claims the 1-1/e guarantee.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 1-1/e guarantee applies to plain greedy on the monotone coverage objective. It does not transfer cleanly to the target-weighted variant, where argmax of (1 + 2 dT) times marginal is not greedy on the reach objective. A multi-hop extension would replace p with an L-step walk weight on the kernel; on the cosponsor graph that is a heuristic reach score (D-025), not an introduction probability, and must not reintroduce the rejected per-edge volume normalization. Weak.
bearings.verifier_note: Corollary 1 and the one-hop coverage update were reproduced. Softened: cost-bounded is a misnomer; the paper does not test one-step heuristics, so the outperformance clause is not supported as a one-step comparison; the 1-1/e claim does not cover the target-weighted variant.

bearings.paper_claim: As seed selectors, plain centralities are weaker than random-walk column sums with saturation. In Table 1, Degree and Betweenness fall below RWCS, GC-RWCS and InfMax, and PageRank is intermediate.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.1 baselines and Section 5.2 Table 1, pp.679-681
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark computes Katz-Bonacich centrality b = (I - delta A)^-1 1 with delta = 0.85 over the spectral radius, on the live kernel P = build_P(adj), counting weighted out-walks. It is a Spearman diagnostic only and no chain step consumes it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper concerns GNN attack selection on citation benchmarks, not legislators, so it is context only. KB and walk-sum scores remain heuristic outputs (D-025). The defensible transfer is narrower: unsaturated walk sums (RWCS) are not a strong selection rule in this paper, which is consistent with keeping KB diagnostic only.
bearings.verifier_note: The ordering claim is contradicted by Table 1. Degree and Betweenness give lower post-attack accuracy, meaning stronger attacks, than RWCS and PageRank in all 18 setups, and are weaker than GC-RWCS and both InfMax methods in all 18. PageRank is the weakest baseline (highest post-attack accuracy) in 14 of 18 setups and RWCS in 4. Means over 18 setups: PageRank 74.5, RWCS 74.1, Betweenness 67.6, Degree 67.0, GC-RWCS 62.5, InfMax-Unif 61.1, InfMax-Norm 61.0. The code description holds: diagnostic only, delta scaled by the spectral radius.

bearings.paper_claim: Perturbing features of only 1 percent of nodes, chosen by an influence-maximization criterion, sharply lowers accuracy of GCN, GAT and JK-Net. Cora GAT falls from 87.7 (no attack) to 55.9 under InfMax-Unif at the 10 percent degree threshold. The paper's model (B = M^L) implies that propagation lets a few nodes affect many predictions; no propagation ablation is reported.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.675; Section 5.2 Table 1 pp.680-681; Section 4.2 Eq. 4-5 p.677-678
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation takes the one-hop mean TSCORE of at least 5 labelled cosponsor neighbours and keeps proposals with |est| at least 0.75. The masking validation sign agreement is stored in data/stance/stance_dynamics.json as 0.775 over n = 1087. Proposals go to a CSV only; the matrix is unchanged.
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py: lines 131-146 (MINNB, CONF, neighbour mean, proposals); lines 143-157 (masking validation and JSON output)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system has no GNN and uses a one-hop mean with human adjudication, so propagation is shallow and an adversary is implausible. The transferable idea is a sensitivity test: flip or corrupt the labels of a few high-coverage members, chosen by walk coverage rather than at random, and count sign changes in the proposals. Any result stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062). Weak.
bearings.verifier_note: The Table 1 numbers were reproduced (Cora GAT 87.7, 55.9, GC-RWCS 57.5). The 5-neighbour and 0.75 thresholds were confirmed in the code. The 77 percent figure matches the stored 0.775 (n = 1087, file dated 2026-07-01). Softened: the sentence that propagation is what lets few nodes affect many predictions is the analyst's inference, not a tested result. The runtime print still says at least 3 neighbours, a stale message.

related.why: Its item states that complex contagion with S-shaped adoption breaks submodularity, which is the non-concave-threshold case where Proposition 2 does not apply. Verified against the item's theory field; the Chen text itself was not re-read here.
Title matches a competitive threshold-model paper, where submodularity can fail. The Ma et al. result gives the single-campaign condition. Item title checked only; the content was not re-read here.

Almazaydeh argues centrality heuristics challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization. Ma et al. find Degree, Betweenness and PageRank weaker than greedy-type selectors on this coverage objective. The two papers study different objectives, so this is a tension rather than a direct contradiction.
Title shows Kumar uses a GNN to solve influence maximization, while Ma et al. use influence maximization to attack a GNN. The item was checked by title only.
Item describes a temporal GNN stance model with silent-user information. If such a model is adopted, the node-perturbation vulnerability shown by Ma et al. becomes a direct robustness question.

summary_issues: Summary says Degree and Betweenness are the weakest baselines. Table 1 shows they beat RWCS and PageRank in every one of 18 setups. PageRank is the weakest baseline in 14 of 18 setups and RWCS in 4.

Summary and bearing repeat the paper's count that both proposed methods beat all baselines in all but 3 of 18 setups. Not reproduced: strict both-method wins occur in 14 of 18 setups; best-method wins in 17 of 18.

Summary says Paul's frontier and coalition allocators use lazy greedy over Monte Carlo spread. per_topic_coalition.py uses singleton marginals with water-filling and no greedy loop; budget_frontier.py has no lazy, CELF or greedy term by grep. Unsupported as written.

Guarantee wording: submodularity and the greedy guarantee apply to the expected objective h(S) under the threshold assumptions, not to the realized misclassification rate. The paper leaves concentration open (Section 4.4).

The Paul alignment note (margin note on Chen 2023, static and submodular tier, GCOMB and CELF expectations) cannot be checked from this item. paul_entries is empty and no annotation exists for this work, so it should not enter the vault as a finding about this paper.
The golovin-2011 link (builds-on) is unsupported: Ma et al. do not cite Golovin or Krause. Dropped from related.
The stance bearing sentence that propagation is what lets few nodes affect many predictions is an inference from the model, not a tested result. Softened in its verdict.

Summary says the greedy guarantee holds only when each threshold CDF is concave. Proposition 2 is a sufficient condition, not an if-and-only-if, and Lemma 1 is an unconditional hardness result for the deterministic problem. The same overstatement appears in the rel gaps field.
